title: Silent Alarm: Catching Quantization's Hidden Safety Cost with J-Space
hook: Quantizing a model to save memory can quietly gut its internal danger-recognition circuitry — even when its answers on safety benchmarks look unchanged.
key_points: JADR reads a model's internal 'danger recognition' from J-space activations before a single response token — no external judge needed.
Tested on 6 models (Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B, Qwen3-Uncensored-4B, Qwen3-SafeRL-4B, Gemma 2 9B) across BF16, INT8, and INT4 quantization.
The SafetyAUC metric statistically separates models with strong vs. weak internal safety mechanisms, with bootstrap confidence intervals.
Quantization degrades this internal signal by substantively different amounts across models — a risk response-based safety evals can miss.
Lands amid a wider community response to Anthropic's Jacobian-Lens release, including visualizer tools and follow-up experiments.
content_html: Most jailbreak-robustness research grades safety by reading a model's generated responses through an LLM judge — sensitive to the grading procedure, and blind to why a model's defenses are fragile. This paper measures danger recognition directly from the model's own activations, before it writes a single word.
extra_html: JADR (Jacobian Assessment of Danger Recognition) builds on J-space, a workspace of verbalizable concepts recently introduced through Anthropic's Jacobian-Lens interpretability method. For each prompt and layer, the authors record the top J-space tokens, group them into six behavioral scenario axes, and compare a danger sample (from StrongREJECT) against safe controls (XSTest, OKTest) — entirely from local activations, with no external judge model. Applied to six models (Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B, Qwen3-Uncensored-4B, Qwen3-SafeRL-4B, Gemma 2 9B) across BF16, INT8, and INT4 quantization, their SafetyAUC metric statistically separates strong from weak internal safety mechanisms and shows quantization degrades that internal signal by substantively different amounts across models — a fragility that behavioral, response-based safety evals can miss entirely. The paper lands amid a broader wave of community activity around Anthropic's Jacobian-Lens release, including third-party visualizer/steering tools and follow-up entropy-based error-detection experiments — a sign the underlying method is quickly becoming a shared toolkit for probing model internals. Roman Prosvirnin and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

related.title: The Illusion of Equivalency: Why 'Same Accuracy' Doesn't Mean 'Same Model'
related.hook: Two quantized models can score identically on accuracy while disagreeing on which individual examples they get right — a gap standard benchmarks are structurally blind to.

related.title: Internal-State Probes Read the Situation, Not the Action
related.hook: Probes that seem to detect an LLM's harmful intent before it acts mostly just detect the prompt's topic — three careful tests find they don't predict future misbehavior.

flashcards.prompt: What does JADR measure, and when does it measure it?
flashcards.back_html: A model's internal danger-recognition representation in J-space, measured from local activations before the model generates its first response token.

flashcards.prompt: Why is measuring J-space activations an advantage over typical LLM-as-judge safety evals?

choices.text: It runs on the evaluated model's own local activations, needing no external judge and capturing hidden mechanism, not just output behavior
It requires running the model on many more prompts than judge-based evals
It only works on models that have never been fine-tuned

flashcards.explanation_html: Judge-based evals only see generated responses and inherit the grader's own biases; JADR reads the internal representation directly, before any output exists.

flashcards.prompt: What did JADR reveal about quantization's effect on safety that behavioral evals might miss?
flashcards.back_html: Quantizing a model (BF16 to INT8/INT4) can weaken its internal danger-recognition mechanism by different amounts per model, even if safety scores look stable.
